**Comprehension (Q. 96 - 100):** Few people truly understand the hidden life of the street. Even when we enter it, we often fail to recognise the unique individuals who belong to it— the wanderers and nomads who have preserved their secrets through generations. We understand even less about the street at night, when it resembles a great house whose doors are locked. Charles Dickens, however, understood the street deeply. He seemed to possess the key to its hidden world. The street lamps were his stars, and the ordinary person on the street was his hero. He could reveal its innermost character and enter its secret passages, lined with houses and roofed with stars. Facts that are merely observed do not remain permanently fixed in memory. To remember a place forever, one must experience it completely and become so deeply absorbed in it that one temporarily forgets oneself as a separate observer. For Dickens, the streets remained deeply romantic because they were 11 associated with the powerful experiences and tragedies of his youth. They were also filled with memories of sunsets that could never return. This emotional connection explains the unusual realism with which he brought the dark and ordinary corners of London to life. In his descriptions, even minor details—a window, a railing or the keyhole of a door —acquire an intense and lifelike vitality. Through his imagination, ordinary objects appear more vivid and real than they normally do.

---

According to the passage, what distinguished Dickens's understanding of the street?
option_a: He studied the architectural features of London in great detail.
option_b: He viewed the street mainly as a setting for dramatic events.
option_c: He observed street life from a safe and emotional distance.
option_d: He understood the hidden life and character of the street deeply.
